noi_dung:
The Chan Hall Is the Way-Place That Selects Buddhas

Everyone coming to the Chan Hall to apply effort may be seen as sitting for an examination—testing who will win the fruition of Buddhahood. How can one pass? The crux is reaching the state "within, no body or mind; without, no world"—in other words, this state:

Seeing, yet not seeing;

Hearing, yet not hearing;

Smelling, yet no scent.

Whoever has such skill has hope of passing.

Why seeing, yet not seeing? Through "returning the light and reflecting it inward." Why hearing, yet not hearing? Through "turning the hearing around to listen to oneself." Why smelling, yet no scent? Because body and mind are gathered in, so scents cause no clinging. This is the state where the eyes see forms yet see no forms, the ears hear sounds as if no sounds, the nose smells scents yet senses no scent, the tongue tastes yet no flavor, the body touches yet feels nothing, the mind meets dharmas yet clings to no dharmas. Only reaching this state is there hope of passing and becoming a Buddha. Only when "in the blazing furnace, still fresh and green" (the furnace fire all blue), standing on the "lofty mountain peak," at the "hundred-foot pole's tip" yet leaping further—only then is there hope. So in the Chan Hall we cannot waste time. The ancients said:

An inch of time, an inch of gold;

An inch of gold cannot buy an inch of time.

Gold lost may yet be found;

Time lost—where to seek?

We must seize the moment and strive in cultivation. Many are the Dharma-doors, but "investigating Chan" alone is supreme. In this Dharma-door, applying effort to ripeness can work a total turnaround—can "turn the back on dust to unite with awakening"—and pass to become a Buddha.

The Bodhisattva-Way cultivator can give up country, home, wife and children. Within the body, he can even give up head, eyes, brains and marrow—wholeheartedly for beings, giving all without regret. Equipped with such a spirit, at the "Buddha-selecting school" there is hope of passing. Know that this is the Buddhas' selection—utterly impartial, won by no luck but only by your own true skill.

Buddhas select Buddhas—not demons selecting Buddhas—yet demons aid Buddhas. Buddhas teach beings directly, while demons teach indirectly, teaching from the reverse side, spurring us to great vows and aiding our vigorous cultivation. So demons are the other face of Good Knowing Advisors. I often say:

Demons whet the path of the Way;

The True Way always has demons.

The more whet, the brighter;

The brighter, the more whetting.

Whet like the bright moon

Shining mid-sky upon the demon host;

Its light scattering demons—

The original Buddha appears.

So we should not treat demons as enemies, but regard demons as Good Knowing Advisors too. Contemplating thus, we rest at ease and avoid afflictions. For example, someone speaking ill of us is our Good Knowing Advisor. Doing a thing rightly, yet told we did it wrong—we strive to do it still more rightly, as in the saying: "Atop the hundred-foot pole, step one step further." "Whoever shows me my faults is my teacher"—we must regard whoever finds our faults as our teacher, thanking them, not taking them for enemies.

The Buddhas are not as muddled as we are; so while we keep wearing our false faces, we can never be selected as Buddhas. We must sincerely seek what is true—and true, yet truer still—we must be "true, true, true, true, true, true, true!" seven times true, to hope for selection. That is "seven trues, eighth right"—in the seven-day Chan Session, genuinely cultivate; on the eighth day, reform from wrong to right. Then all foul habits are swept away at once, reaching utter purity!

Chan Session talks, December 1980 What Is a "No-Mind Cultivator"?

In the Sutra in Forty-Two Chapters there is a line: "Feeding the Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions cannot match feeding a no-mind cultivator." What is a no-mind cultivator? It means the Chan investigator in the Chan Hall who has no mind seeking fame or gain—who has cut off the five roots of the hells: wealth, sex, fame, food, and sleep—with no mind, no other thoughts, while sitting investigating Chan. Such a one is called a no-mind cultivator.

To truly propagate the Dharma in this West, we must follow the "no-mind cultivator" Dharma-door. This is not hoping for offerings for "no-mind cultivators"—for a mind set on offerings is already having a mind. So Chan Hall time is time we truly practice Chan and samadhi—never letting discursive thoughts surge one after another, like film frames flickering past—that is a hundred and eight thousand miles from the Way. The further you walk, the farther from home; you become a wandering vagrant—how pitiable!

We must strive genuinely in cultivation, relying only on our own true skill. Crave no fame or gain; avoid advertising yourselves. Cultivate in the spirit of Manjushri, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteshvara, Ksitigarbha, and the Bodhisattvas—protecting the Way-place and teaching beings. The Bodhisattvas ever take the accomplishment of beings as their own accomplishment, with no distinction of self and others. Bodhisattvas ever hear of people's merit and rejoice in praising it.

The proverb says: "With musk, fragrance comes of itself—what need to fan it with a great wind?" The cultivator mindless to a high degree naturally wins sympathetic response. Doing the Buddha's work is being a Buddha; doing a Bodhisattva's work is being a Bodhisattva; doing an Arhat's work is being an Arhat; doing a ghost's work is being a ghost—that is only natural. The cultivator of the Way cannot take shortcuts or rely on luck. Only truly committing, step by steady step, sincerely cultivating, may one hope one day to accomplish the Way-karma.

Chan Session talks, December 1980
